questions.prompt: How does the composite SLA of two services that depend on each other in series compare with each service alone?

options.text: It is higher than either service
It is lower, because the SLAs multiply together
It is exactly the same as each service
SLAs cannot be combined at all

questions.explanation: In series, SLAs multiply into a lower composite (e.g., 99.9% × 99.9% ≈ 99.8%). Parallel redundancy is what raises effective availability.

questions.prompt: Which statements about reliability and scaling are true? Select all that apply.

options.text: Availability zones protect against a whole-datacenter outage
Scaling out adds more instances behind a load balancer
Autoscale can add/remove instances based on metrics or a schedule
Scaling up has no practical upper limit

questions.explanation: Zones protect against datacenter outages; scaling out adds instances; autoscale reacts to metrics/schedules. Scaling up has a ceiling — scale out for elasticity and resilience.

questions.prompt: The measure of how much data loss you can tolerate (how far back your last good copy is) is abbreviated ____.
questions.explanation: RPO (Recovery Point Objective) is tolerable data loss; RTO (Recovery Time Objective) is tolerable downtime. Design backup/DR to meet both.

questions.prompt: Order these from LEAST to MOST resilient.
questions.explanation: Resilience grows from a single instance, to an availability set (rack/maintenance protection), to zones (datacenter outage), to multiple regions (regional disaster).

questions.prompt: Match each reliability concept to its meaning.

pairs.right: The provider's uptime commitment for a service
VMs spread across fault/update domains in one datacenter
VMs spread across separate datacenters in a region
How quickly you must be back online

questions.explanation: An SLA is the uptime commitment; availability sets protect within a datacenter; zones protect across datacenters; RTO is tolerable downtime.
